com: There was silence in heaven: which is to represent as it were a general consternation, and an expectation of dreadful events at the opening of the seventh seal, and when seven Angels stood prepared to sound seven trumpets. (Witham)

Stood before the altar, having a golden censer. In the visions is an allusion to the tabernacle and its parts. The altar of perfumes was in the sanctum[the holy place], hard by the entrance into the sanctum sanctorum[the holy of holies], and here the golden altar is said to be before the throne of God. The incense from the censer is said to be the prayers of all the Saints, which the Angel offered up. The altar seems to signify our Saviour Christ, as the prayers of all the faithful are always made through the merits of Christ, our only chief Mediator or Redeemer. By the fire cast upon the earth, (ver. 5.) is signified the fire of divine charity, now to be exercised by the ways of justice, to draw persons to their conversion by punishments. (Witham) — We may observe both in this and other places of the Apocalypse, that St. John makes continual allusions to what was done in the temple of Jerusalem, for which he gives us symbolical reasons. Thus on the present occasion, the incense which was offered morning and evening in the temple, on the golden altar, is represented as done here in heaven. (Calmet)

The first Angel sounded, &c. From this place to the eleventh verse of chapter xx. the visions are differently expounded. Some interpret them, without applying them to any particular events, as general comminations, in a mystical and allegorical sense of the many persecutions which God permits to happen to his Church. Others think that they are all predictions, which shall not happen till a little time before the end of the world, in antichrist’s time, after which will follow the day of the general judgment, the punishment of the wicked, and the reward of the just. But there are others, both ancient and later writers, as in particular Alcazar, the bishop of Meaux (Bossuet,) Pere Alleman, to whom we may add among the Protestants, Dr. Hammond, whom the bishop of Meaux calls the most learned of all the English Protestants. According to the interpretations which these writers have followed, these predictions of St. John (except the last persecution, when the devil shall be let loose, Chap. xx. 7, in the time of the great antichrist) have already happened in the three first ages[centuries], during the persecutions of the heathen emperors, as I shall briefly take notice. Hail therefore, and fire, blood, falling of stars, &c. some look upon as mystical representations, to signify that a great many trials and persecutions shall happen to the good, and a great many punishments and chastisements shall fall upon the wicked; with this grand difference, that the sufferings of the good shall be short and momentary, and their reward a crown of endless glory; but the wicked, if any of them escape punishments in this world, can never escape eternal torments with the devils in the next. 2. It is also a very common opinion, that all these disasters shall happen in a great measure, literally about antichrist’s time, a very short time before the end of the world. 3. Others apply all these events to the judgments which God’s justice exercised either upon the Jews, in the time of Trajan and Adrian, or upon the heathen Roman emperors, and upon the pagan city of Rome, for persecuting the servants of God. (Witham) — As these Angels with their trumpets, according to Pastorini, denote the sufferings of the Church during the seven ages that it lasts, it may not be improper to point out the time, according to his opinion, when each Angel sounded the trumpet. Thus the first trumpet denotes the persecutions of the first three centuries, in which the Christians suffered death by the sword, (denoted by blood) by being stoned, (denoted by the hail) and by fire, when the third part of the trees were burnt, that is, the third part of the clergy were destroyed. (Pastorini)
The great mountain denotes the heresy of Arius, which caused the greatest troubles in the Church, and destroyed many churches, which are here denoted by the ships. (Pastorini)

A great star fell. The bishop of Meaux [Bossuet] thinks this agrees very well to Cochebas, or Barcochebas, who in Adrian’s time pretended to be the true Messias of the Jews; his name also signifying a star. He was the chief cause of those wars, and of the utter destruction of the Jews. (Witham) — The third trumpet points out to us the punishment that falls upon the Roman empire, in its destruction by the northern nations. These people spread themselves over the third part of the rivers and provinces of ancient Rome. The star is called wormwood, from the bitter calamities and miseries which they inflicted upon the Roman empire. (Pastorini)

The third part of the sun was smitten. This may signify a third part of men killed in those wars, or (according to the opinion that refers all to antichrist’s time) that in those days the sun and moon shall not give above a third part of their light. (Witham) — Here we behold a noble figure of the Church, which whilst in its most flourishing state, like the sun, is suddenly obscured, and a third part extinguished by the heresy and schism of the Greeks, under Photius, which began in 866[A.D. 866], and infected all orders of Christians, clergy and laity, princes and individuals, signified by the sun, moon, and stars. (Pastorini)

The voice of one eagle: in divers Greek copies, of an Angel, saying, Woe, woe, woe! It is to foretell, in general, greater punishments and miseries. The Protestant translation has followed those Greek copies that read an Angel; but Dr. Wells, in his amendments, has restored that reading of an eagle which the ancient Latin interpreter had met with. (Witham) — An eagle, on account of its swiftness, is here represented as chosen to announce by its cry of woe on the three succeeding ages of the Church, greater disasters to be sustained than in the preceding ages. (Pastorini)
fa: Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

"And when He had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour." Whereby is signified the beginning of everlasting rest; but it is described as partial, because the silence being interrupted, he repeats it in order. For if the silence had continued, here would be an end of his narrative.
Commentary on Revelation

And when he had opened the seventh seal. The opening of the seventh seal refers to the birth of Christ; but we must ask why it is placed in the seventh place, and not in the fifth. In Genesis it is written that in six days God made all things that took their origin from heaven and earth, but on the seventh He rested; and therefore He called the seventh day “sabbath,” that is, “rest” (Gen. 2:2). But what is our rest, if not Christ? …
Commentary on Revelation

There was silence in heaven for about half an hour. By this silence is signified the peace that, with the birth of Christ, was established throughout the whole world by Octavian Augustus. But the silence was for about half an hour, because the peace which the Church had among the pagans at the beginning of the faith lasted only a short time; for it was broken by the emperor Nero, and after Peter and Paul were killed, he ordered that all Christians be persecuted.
Commentary on Revelation

And I saw seven angels standing in the presence of God, and seven trumpets were given to them. The order of these seven angels is shown in what follows; for just as an announcer is sent before a king or prince to announce his coming, so also John, because the things signified through the angels were great, wished to call them to mind before he came to relate their story.
On Prayer

To this is further added the charge of irreverence,-intelligible even to the nations themselves, if they had any sense. If, on the one hand, it is irreverent to sit under the eye, and over against the eye, of him whom you most of all revere and venerate; how much more, on the other hand, is that deed most irreligious under the eye of the living God, while the angel Of prayer is still standing by unless we are upbraiding God that prayer has wearied us!
Commentary on Revelation

Then another angel came and stood before the altar, having a golden censer in his hand; and much incense was given to him, that he might offer from the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the Lord. This angel signifies Christ; he came because through the mystery of the Incarnation he appeared in the world. By the golden altar the Church is indicated. He is said to have stood before the altar; for Christ lay prostrate among unbelievers, who considered him a mere man; but he stood among the faithful, who believed that he was truly God. …
Commentary on Revelation

And the smoke of the incense went up from the prayers of the saints, from the hand of the angel before the sight of God. By the smoke of the incense not only the prayers of the faithful are signified, but also the fragrance of good works, which unceasingly rises from the Church before the sight of God. This smoke is said to ascend from the hand of the angel, because whatever good the faithful do, they do with God working in them, as He Himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (Jn. 15:5).
Commentary on Revelation

And the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar, and cast it upon the earth. And there were lightnings, voices, and thunderings, and an earthquake. By fire the Holy Spirit is signified: therefore the angel, that is, Christ, filled the censer, that is, the hearts of the disciples, with fire from the altar, that is, with the Holy Spirit; when, after his ascension into heaven, on the tenth day, with the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, he filled the hearts of the disciples and gave them knowledge of all languages. …
Commentary on Revelation

By the abundance of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have said a little about the openings of the seven seals; now let us bring forward some points about the sounding of the trumpets of the seven angels which follows. By the seven angels are signified the teachers who have been sent by God, and will be sent until the end, to instruct the people of God. …
Commentary on Revelation

And the seven angels prepared themselves to sound the trumpets. By the sounding of the trumpet, preaching is signified; for the holy preachers are always ready for this purpose, that by the teaching of their preaching they may win for God whomever they can.
Commentary on Revelation

And the first angel sounded the trumpet. By the first angel, as we have already said, the preachers who were before the Law are indicated. Therefore the first angel sounded the trumpet, because the holy men who lived before the Law, although they had no law except the natural one, are believed to have urged whomever they could to this: that they should fear and love God their creator, and that what someone would not wish to suffer, he should not do to another.
Commentary on Revelation

And there came hail and fire, mixed with blood, and it was sent upon the earth. The things that were seen to have happened when the seven angels sounded the trumpets are, in my view, to be taken in a good sense; just as, on the contrary, the pouring out of the bowls of the seven angels which follows is to be taken in a bad sense. Therefore, by the hail that strikes, the words of the holy men are indicated, which, by reproving, struck the hearts of wicked people. …
Commentary on Revelation

… 20:17), as Abimelech through Abraham, and through Job his three friends (Job 42:8). By the green grass, however, which is said to be all burned, those are indicated who above were meant by the third part of the earth and the trees that were burned, that is, the elect who lived at that time; for green grass is hard to set on fire, but dry grass is easily consumed. By the green grass, then, the elect are signified, and by the dry, the wicked. Of this dry grass the prophet says: “Truly the people are grass. The grass is dried up and the flower has fallen; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:7). …
Commentary on Revelation
And the second angel sounded the trumpet. By the second angel Moses and the other teachers of the Law are signified.
Commentary on Revelation

And behold, as it were a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea. By the great mountain the Law of Moses is signified, which, because of the weight of its burden, is likened to a mountain; and because of the spiritual understanding that shone forth in the Law, it is said to burn with fire. The Hebrew people themselves, because of the magnitude of their crimes, are signified by the sea.
Commentary on Revelation

… 24:8). Therefore, by the third part of the sea, those chosen ones who lived at that time are signified; and by blood in this passage we may understand the remission of sins. Therefore the third part of the sea was turned into blood, because the elect who were then alive deserved to be cleansed from their sins through the observance of the Law. The third part of the creatures that had life in the sea, which is said to have died, has the same meaning as the third part of the sea that was turned into blood. …
Commentary on Revelation

And the third angel blew the trumpet, and a star burning like a torch fell from heaven. The star has the same meaning as the angel; for it signifies the prophets. But we must ask how it is said to have fallen from heaven to earth. The saints in a certain way ascend to heaven when divine love lifts them up to contemplate heavenly things; they fall to earth when love for their neighbors draws them back down, so that by their preaching they may lead sinners back to the way of truth. A torch, moreover, is lit to drive away the darkness of the night. …
Commentary on Revelation

And it fell upon a third part of the rivers and upon the springs of waters. By the rivers and springs the twelve tribes with their families are represented; by the third part, those among them are figured who were marked out for eternal life. The star therefore fell upon the third part of the rivers, because those who were predestined to eternal life received the teaching of the prophets and planted it in their hearts.
Commentary on Revelation

And the name of the star is called wormwood. Wormwood is very bitter; by wormwood, therefore, are signified the threats of the prophets, which they directed against the sinning people, declaring to them that unless they repent, they would be given over as spoil and into captivity to their enemies; and that if even then they did not repent, they would be condemned to eternal death.
Commentary on Revelation

And a third part of the waters was turned into wormwood. Those whom we said above were signified by the third part of the waters, that is, the elect, received the bitterness of penance through the threats of the prophets.
Commentary on Revelation

And many men died from the waters, because they were made bitter. For the bitterness of penance brought death to those who deserved to be saved; for they died according to what was evil in them, and lived according to what they began to be in goodness.
Commentary on Revelation
And the fourth angel sounded the trumpet. The fourth angel signifies Christ and his apostles.
Commentary on Revelation

And a third part of the sun was struck, and a third part of the moon, and a third part of the stars, so that a third part of them was darkened, and a third part of the day did not shine, and likewise of the night. The sun, the moon, and the stars all refer to one thing; for by the sun the people of the Jews are signified, by the moon the Synagogue, and by the stars the leaders of the priests and the Pharisees. But if we should wish to transfer the darkening of the sun and moon and stars to those who were unwilling to believe in Christ, the order established above will be disturbed. …
Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

"And I saw an angel flying through the midst of heaven." By the angel flying through the midst of heaven is signified the Holy Spirit beating witness in two of the prophets that a great wrath of plagues was imminent. If by any means, even in the last times, any one should be willing to be converted, any one might even still be saved.
Commentary on Revelation

And I saw and heard the voice of one eagle flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice: Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the voices of the three angels who were about to sound the trumpet. By “heaven” in this place the Church is signified, while the eagle signifies Christ and His apostles. The eagle, then, was flying through the midst of heaven and crying out, because Christ first through Judaea, and His apostles through all the nations, preached the Gospel; and they also foretold in many ways what persecutions from adversaries the Church would have to endure. …
ftr: John Litteral, released into the public domain
